findings.title: Device is cached as tagged before the limit check, so a rejected device is admitted on its next request
findings.body: tagDeviceUI sets the local cache entry for the device before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice, and never removes it when the store fails. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate rejects the request, but the device key stays cached for the default 29-minute expiry. The device's next request hits the cache check at the top of tagDeviceUI, returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds without any database record. A rejected device is therefore admitted on retry and stays admitted for up to ~29 minutes, so the configured device limit is not enforced for that device. The cache entry should only be set after a successful tag, or be deleted when CreateOrUpdateDevice returns an error.

findings.title: Device limit keys off a client-supplied, unverified header
findings.body: The device identity is the raw X-Grafana-Device-Id request header, accepted without any server-side verification. A client that sends a fresh ID on each request is counted as a new device every time, so the cap can be bypassed trivially. Clearing browser storage has the same effect. If the limit is meant to be enforced rather than advisory, the device identity needs a server-verifiable basis; otherwise the limit should be documented as not being a security control.

findings.title: Limit check is a separate COUNT followed by a separate insert, so concurrent requests can exceed the limit
findings.body: The check at lines 110-116 counts devices, then the insert/upsert runs later in a separate statement with no transaction or lock. Concurrent first requests from different new devices can all read count < deviceLimit and all insert, so the stored device count can overshoot the configured limit by up to the number of concurrent requests. The limit is only soft under load. If it is meant to be strict, the check and insert must be atomic (for example a conditional insert within a transaction).

findings.title: Device tagging moved from a background goroutine onto the synchronous auth path
findings.body: Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout and panic recovery, so anonymous authentication never waited on the database. Now it runs inline with the request context. Each device that misses the local cache (the first request per device and again every ~29 minutes) performs a COUNT(*) over the 30-day window plus an upsert or update before the request can be authenticated. With many devices or a slow database this adds latency to those requests and holds request goroutines and DB connections. The cap check makes this worse because it adds a COUNT to the hot path. Consider keeping the non-blocking write for the normal path, or bounding the synchronous call with a timeout.

findings.title: Tests only cover rejection of a new device at the limit, not the update path or the authentication flow
findings.body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a brand-new device is rejected when the table is at the limit. Not covered: (a) an existing in-window device being updated successfully while the limit is reached, which is the updateDevice success path; (b) devices outside the 30-day window not being counted; (c) TagDevice or Authenticate actually returning ErrDeviceLimitReached to the caller; (d) a rejected device retrying. The retry bug in impl.go (device cached after rejection) would be caught by a test that calls TagDevice twice for a rejected device.

findings.title: RowsAffected()==0 used as 'device not found' is unreliable on MySQL
findings.body: updateDevice treats RowsAffected()==0 as meaning the device is not in the window, and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. MySQL reports changed rows by default (unless clientFoundRows is set on the connection), so an UPDATE that sets the same client_ip and user_agent and a updated_at with the same second-precision value reports 0 even though the row matched. In that case an existing, legitimate device is wrongly rejected. The window is narrow (a same-second retag), so the impact is limited, but the check should not rely on affected rows on MySQL, for example by verifying existence with a SELECT.

findings.title: New [auth.anonymous] device_limit option is undocumented
findings.body: The new device_limit option is read here, but the PR does not touch conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini or the docs, and the docs checkbox in the PR description is unchecked. Operators cannot discover that 0 means unlimited, or that the limit counts devices seen within a rolling 30-day window.
